lessons.title: Approaching Logical Puzzles
lessons.concept: Logical puzzles require deducing information from a set of clues. A systematic approach—reading all clues, identifying direct facts, using tables/diagrams, and eliminating impossibilities—helps avoid confusion and missed constraints.
lessons.formula: Steps: list entities/attributes -> note direct clues -> represent with table/grid -> apply constraints -> deduce stepwise -> verify all clues.
lessons.worked_example: If A sits left of B and B sits left of C in a row of three, arrangement is A, B, C. Each clue reduces possible positions until the answer is determined.
mistakes: Not revisiting earlier clues after new deductions
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Using Elimination and Constraints
lessons.concept: Many puzzles are solved by eliminating options that violate constraints. Track what is possible and impossible for each entity. Contradictions indicate an incorrect assumption or missed clue interpretation.
lessons.formula: Constraint handling: mark definite matches, cross out impossible matches, propagate implications from each deduction.
lessons.worked_example: Three people P,Q,R have different pets cat,dog,fish. If P does not have cat and R has dog, then P cannot have dog/cat so P has fish, and Q has cat.
mistakes: Stopping before all clues are satisfied
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Verification and Consistency
lessons.concept: After reaching a solution, verify it against every given clue. A valid solution must satisfy all constraints simultaneously. If any clue is violated, revisit deductions to find the error or missed case.
lessons.formula: Final check: for each clue -> solution satisfies clue? All must be true.
lessons.worked_example: If a seating answer states X is left of Y but a clue requires Y to be left of X, the arrangement is inconsistent and must be corrected.
mistakes: Ignoring implicit relations derived from multiple clues
Accepting first arrangement found without full verification

practice.question: In a puzzle, A, B, C have colors red, blue, green. A has red, B does not have green. What color does B have?
practice.explanation: A has red, so B cannot have red. B does not have green, so B must have blue (and C has green).

practice.question: The most reliable first move in a seating/arrangement puzzle is to:

options.A: Place people randomly to fill the grid
options.B: Anchor a definite clue (relative position with no freedom) as your starting point
options.D: Solve option by option without a table

practice.explanation: Definite clues ('X sits opposite Y', 'A is immediately next to B on the left') fix positions with zero ambiguity; building from them constrains the rest of the puzzle quickly.

practice.question: Negative clues such as 'C does not sit next to D' are used mainly to:

options.B: Eliminate placements already suggested by positive clues

practice.explanation: Positive clues construct possibilities; negative clues prune them. Both are required - pruning is what makes contradictory placements detectable.

options.B: Test each against every remaining clue; keep only fully consistent assignments

questions.explanation: Consistency verification against ALL constraints (including negative ones) is the final filter; only assignments satisfying every clue can be the keyed solution.

questions.question: A puzzle states there is exactly one valid arrangement. What does that imply about the clues?

options.B: The clue set must be sufficient to reduce candidates to exactly one
options.C: Some clues may contradict each other
options.D: Order of clue application does not matter only by luck

questions.explanation: Uniqueness means the clues jointly eliminate every arrangement but one; exam setters check sufficiency. Contradictions (zero solutions) or ambiguity (many solutions) both indicate a solving error.

questions.question: Which clue type is most dangerous to misread in arrangement puzzles?
questions.explanation: 'Immediately to the left of' is directional and unique; 'is a neighbour of' allows either side. Confusing them creates phantom placements - the most common puzzle error.
